sentences.text: Every species of this extinct genus grew to a length ranging from three to five meters.
One specific specimen, cataloged as PMO 222.655, was estimated to measure between 3.8 and 4.3 meters.
Its skull featured a snout that was very short yet robust relative to the total head length.
The eye socket occupied a space approximately 0.34 times the length of the entire skull.
This animal possessed a pineal foramen that was proportionately larger than that of any other known ophthalmosaurid.
The shaft of the upper arm bone narrowed to about 20% of its maximum width at the midpoint.
The lower end of the humerus was larger than the upper end and carried three joint surfaces, one of which formed a 120° angle with the radial facet.
The upper portion of the hip bone was 1.5 times wider than the lower portion near the hip joint, a unique trait for the group.
The fused pelvic bones were uniquely shorter than the thigh bone among members of the Ophthalmosauridae family.
The thigh bone displayed ends of roughly equal width with a slightly narrower middle section.
The genus was first described by Maxwell in the year 2010.
Remains of this animal represent the most complete ichthyosaur fossils ever found in the Canadian Arctic.
A skull and forefin of an ophthalmosaurid were described in 2012 from the Neuquén Basin in Argentina.
The geological layers in Svalbard holding these fossils date to the Volgian stage, roughly matching the Tithonian to early Berriasian periods.
In 2019, Zverkov and Prilepskaya revised the group, deciding that Janusaurus and Palvennia are junior synonyms of Arthropterygius.
Zverkov and Prilepskaya also recognized the taxon Ichthyosaurus volgensis from Russia as a new species, named A. volgensis.
Fossils of A. chrisorum, A. lundi, and A. hoybergeti originate from the Slottsmøya Member of the Agardhfjellet Formation.
The seafloor at the Slottsmøya Member site sat about 150 meters below the surface in relatively oxygen-poor waters.
Researchers suggest that sea ice was likely present at this high-latitude site during winter due to the cool Tithonian climate.
The Slottsmøya Member contains fossils of other marine reptiles including Undorosaurus gorodischensis, Nannopterygius borealis, and Brachypterygius sp.
This formation includes 21 plesiosaurian specimens, with Pliosaurus funkei likely serving as the apex predator.
Four species of Arthropterygius, including A. chrisorum, A. volgensis, A. lundi, and A. hoybergeti, are found in the Volga region of Russia.
The species A. thalassonotus is found in the Vaca Muerta Formation of the Neuquén Basin in Patagonia, Argentina.
Maxwell classified Arthropterygius as the sister taxon to the Argentine ophthalmosaurid Caypullisaurus in 2010.
Many recent cladistic analyses classify Arthropterygius as the basalmost member of the family Ophthalmosauridae.
Arthropterygius chrisorum serves as the type species for the genus Arthropterygius.
Ophthalmosaurus chrisorum is a synonym of Arthropterygius chrisorum.
Fossils of Arthropterygius date from the Kimmeridgian to possibly the Berriasian.
The animal lived during the late Jurassic and possibly into the earliest Cretaceous.
Arthropterygius lived from the Oxfordian to the Tithonian stages, between 161.5 and 143.1 million years ago.
Fossils are found in high-latitude locations across the Northern Hemisphere and one isolated site in Argentina.
It is debated whether the large pineal foramen in Arthropterygius was an adaptation to high-latitude environments.
It is debated whether Janusaurus, Keilhauia, and Palvennia should be treated as synonyms of Arthropterygius, as some studies suggest the evidence does not support this synonymy.
